heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Observe with the senses / Classify living things
details:
1.1.1 Use relevant senses and suitable tools where needed to observe objects, events or changes
1.1.2 Group objects or phenomena by shared and differing characteristics
TB pp. 2-3 · AB pp. 1-2 · TB pp. 4-5 · AB pp. 3

1. Submit three observations and identify sight, touch or hearing beside each.
2. Sort the six pictures independently and write the sorting rule.
Leaves, an opaque sound tube, trays and observation cards.; Six picture cards of living things and two sorting mats.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a leaf and ask which features can be checked without guessing.
Name one feature and say which sense can check it.
Main activity
Set up looking, touching and quiet listening stations. Model the difference between “rough” and “looks old”.
Examine the safe items and record an observation and sense at each station.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to submit three evidence statements and check the sense named for each.
Submit three observations and identify sight, touch or hearing beside each.
Closure
Ask how two pupils can check a disputed observation.
Repeat it using the named sense and report what was observed.
Set induction
Show a bird and a fish. Ask for one feature that can be seen in both images.
Suggest a feature such as legs, fins or a visible covering.
Main activity
Give pairs six animal pictures with clear features. Ask them to name one testable rule and keep it throughout their sort.
Place all six cards into two groups using the named visible feature.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil an unsorted copy and check all six placements against their rule.
Sort the six pictures independently and write the sorting rule.
Closure
Show a new example and ask where it would go.
Place it using the same feature and explain why.
references: TB pp. 2-3 · AB pp. 1-2 · TB pp. 4-5 · AB pp. 3

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Measure and record length
details: 1.1.3 Measure with appropriate tools, standard units and correct techniques, and record numerical readings
1. Measure independently, then submit both lengths in centimetres.
Centimetre rulers, pencils, strips of card and recording slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Hold a strip at the ruler’s 1 cm mark. Ask where its end should start.
Identify the zero mark as the starting point.
Main activity
Model alignment and show how to read the other end in cm. Give each pair two short objects.
Take turns aligning each object at zero, reading the scale and recording the length.
Practice and assessment
Observe each pupil measuring one of the two objects and check both readings and units on the slip.
Measure independently, then submit both lengths in centimetres.
Closure
Show a ruler with a gap before the zero mark.
Explain why the ruler’s edge is different from its zero mark.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Make an inference
details: 1.1.4 Use information from observations to give a reasonable explanation
1. Write one observation and one possible explanation connected by “because”.
Illustrated footprints, comparison cards and an observation–inference sheet.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of damp footprints beside a tap. Ask what the picture actually shows.
Describe one visible detail without suggesting a cause.
Main activity
Model separate observation and inference columns. Give groups two illustrated scenes with more than one possible explanation.
Record visible clues, suggest an explanation for each scene and compare which clues support it.
Practice and assessment
Give an unfamiliar scene to each pupil. Check that the inference is plausible and linked to a visible detail.
Write one observation and one possible explanation connected by “because”.
Closure
Ask for another explanation that fits the same visible evidence.
Offer an alternative and say what could be checked next.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Predict from evidence
details: 1.1.5 Predict an outcome using observations, previous experience, data or patterns
1. Submit a likely next result with one stated pattern or earlier observation.
Three picture cards from a growing pattern, a ruler and prediction slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show three pictures of the same shoot taken on different days.
Describe the pattern across the three pictures.
Main activity
Model using the first two pictures to predict the third. Offer a second sequence with its last picture covered.
Record a prediction and point to a previous result that supports it.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to finish a prediction sentence and give a reason drawn from the sequence.
Submit a likely next result with one stated pattern or earlier observation.
Closure
Reveal the covered result and discuss predictions supported by the pattern.
Compare the result with the prediction and say what evidence was used.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Communicate findings
details: 1.1.6 Record findings in a suitable form and present them systematically
1. Submit a labelled table or drawing and explain one recorded finding.
Shell or leaf cards, magnifiers, paper and sample table headings.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show an unlabelled recording sheet and ask what a reader needs to identify each result.
Suggest a heading, label or key.
Main activity
Model two formats using a different specimen. Give groups specimens or clear photographs and ask them to choose a table or drawing.
Observe three features, record each feature clearly and agree which result to explain.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil’s three observations and ask them to explain one without relying on their partner.
Submit a labelled table or drawing and explain one recorded finding.
Closure
Compare two recordings that present the same idea differently.
Identify one label that helped the reader understand a result.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Communicate findings
details: 1.1.6 Record findings in a suitable form and present them systematically
1. Present three observations of two leaves in a labelled table or drawing; explain one comparison supported by the record.
Shell or leaf cards, magnifiers, paper and sample table headings.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display two leaves and ask which visible difference could be recorded.
Suggest a feature such as shape or leaf edge.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide fresh leaves or clear pictures and a blank data table.
Present three observations of two leaves in a labelled table or drawing; explain one comparison supported by the record.
Closure
Ask for one comparison that refers to the recorded table.
Read a labelled observation and state a supported difference.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Use apparatus and handle specimens
details:
1.2.1 Use and handle science apparatus and materials in the correct way
1.2.2 Handle specimens carefully using suitable techniques
1. Select and use both tools safely, then show the leaf remains intact in the receiving tray.
Magnifiers, blunt tongs, soft brushes, trays and dry leaves.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Compare a crushed paper leaf with an intact one and ask how tools could protect it.
Name a way to hold or move a specimen gently.
Main activity
Demonstrate proper handling of a magnifier and blunt tongs. Set up labelled practice stations with a specimen transfer path.
Inspect a specimen using the magnifier and transfer the specimen between trays without crushing it.
Practice and assessment
Use a three-point checklist for two tools and the specimen transfer. Rotate so each pupil demonstrates independently.
Select and use both tools safely, then show the leaf remains intact in the receiving tray.
Closure
Ask what to do if a fragile part breaks or spills.
Explain how to stop, report and continue after guidance.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Use apparatus and handle specimens
details:
1.2.1 Use and handle science apparatus and materials in the correct way
1.2.2 Handle specimens carefully using suitable techniques
1. Use a hand lens and forceps to observe and move a safe specimen without damaging it; explain two handling rules.
Magnifiers, blunt tongs, soft brushes, trays and dry leaves.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a hand lens and forceps beside a clean specimen.
Identify the tool for viewing detail and the tool for moving the specimen.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Demonstrate tool use and supervise with clean, non-hazardous specimens.
Use a hand lens and forceps to observe and move a safe specimen without damaging it; explain two handling rules.
Closure
Ask how the specimen can be returned without crushing it.
Demonstrate or explain a safe handling action.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Sketch, clean and store
details:
1.2.3 Draw accurate sketches of specimens, apparatus and science materials
1.2.4 Clean science apparatus using the correct method
1.2.5 Put away science apparatus and materials safely in the correct places
1. Show a recognisable sketch with labels and demonstrate the correct clean-and-store sequence.
Specimens, pencils, trays, cleaning cloths, magnifiers and a storage chart.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display a sketch with an unclear label and a tray with equipment in the wrong place.
Suggest one correction to the picture or storage arrangement.
Main activity
Model a clear outline and straight label lines. Demonstrate wiping, drying and returning the apparatus after use.
Observe a specimen, make a labelled sketch, clean the apparatus and match it to its storage place.
Practice and assessment
Check every pupil’s drawing and observe each pupil cleaning and storing one item.
Show a recognisable sketch with labels and demonstrate the correct clean-and-store sequence.
Closure
Ask why damp apparatus is dried before being stored.
Explain one consequence of putting it away wet.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Follow science room rules
details: 2.1.1 Follow the rules for working in the science room
1. Demonstrate an appropriate rule at each stage and explain what could happen if one is ignored.
Science room rules cards, teacher-made scenario cards and empty apparatus trays.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of a crowded doorway and ask how the class should enter safely.
State one action that keeps the entrance clear.
Main activity
Set up a short dry-run with empty trays and rules cards for before, during and after work.
Rehearse entering, handling and returning materials safely. Explain each chosen rule to a partner.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil three situation prompts and use a checklist for the three stages and a consequence.
Demonstrate an appropriate rule at each stage and explain what could happen if one is ignored.
Closure
Ask which rule helps keep the next class safe.
Name a rule and connect it to a possible consequence.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Types of teeth and functions
details: 3.1.1 Describe the different types of teeth and what each does

1. Label all three types and match cutting, tearing and grinding to them.
2. Match pictures of incisors, canines and molars to cutting, tearing and grinding, then explain the function of each.
Tooth model or images, shape cards and job labels.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a pointed and a broad tooth and ask what differences are visible.
Describe the two shapes and propose a job for each.
Main activity
Point to incisors, canines and molars on an image. Use cards to model cutting, tearing and grinding without food handling.
Match each tooth group to its shape and job, then explain one match to a partner.
Practice and assessment
Use three unlabelled images and check the match between name and function for each pupil.
Label all three types and match cutting, tearing and grinding to them.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Give tooth-shape cards and food-action pictures; do not require eating.
Match pictures of incisors, canines and molars to cutting, tearing and grinding, then explain the function of each.
Closure
Ask which tooth is useful for grinding and why its shape helps.
Point to a molar and name its broad surface.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Structure of a tooth
details: 3.1.2 Identify and label the parts of a tooth
1. Label enamel, dentine, gum, blood vessels and nerves on the outline.
Large tooth cross-section, word bank and individual outline cards.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the outside of a tooth and ask what the cutaway view could reveal.
Suggest one part that cannot be seen from outside.
Main activity
Trace the enamel, dentine, gum, blood vessels and nerves on a diagram with five colour-coded prompts.
Place five word cards at the correct sites and compare enamel and dentine positions.
Practice and assessment
Give an unlabelled outline with five arrows. Check each pupil’s labels against the diagram.
Label enamel, dentine, gum, blood vessels and nerves on the outline.
Closure
Ask pupils to point to the outer hard layer and the parts inside the tooth.
Name enamel and distinguish it from the inside structures.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Milk and permanent teeth
details: 3.1.3 Describe similarities and differences between milk teeth and permanent teeth
1. Submit two comparisons with the same feature shown across the two columns.
Milk and permanent tooth-set diagrams, comparison table and counting counters.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two tooth charts with covered headings and ask what can be counted or compared.
Identify one difference visible between charts.
Main activity
Give pairs labelled textbook diagrams to compare quantity, replacement and features visible in the drawings. Model evidence for one cell.
Count and compare the charts, then enter paired observations in a two-column table.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to produce two fair comparisons. Check each comparison refers to both tooth sets.
Submit two comparisons with the same feature shown across the two columns.
Closure
Ask what replaces milk teeth as children grow.
Identify permanent teeth and state one other difference from the table.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Care for teeth and explain why
details:
3.1.4 Explain how dental care protects the different parts of a tooth
3.1.5 Present observations about teeth creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Practise on the model. On a tooth outline, mark where a simulated residue mark changed after brushing.
Tooth model, washable food-residue marks, demonstration brush and tooth outlines.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two dental care routines and ask which protects a tooth and how.
Choose a routine and suggest one reason.
Main activity
Mark the chewing surface and gumline on the model. Demonstrate gentle brushing and compare the marks before and after.
Practise on the model. On a tooth outline, mark where a simulated residue mark changed after brushing.
Closure
Show the before-and-after simulated residue marks on the tooth model.
Identify one area that became cleaner after brushing.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Care for teeth and explain why / Classify foods
details:
3.1.4 Explain how dental care protects the different parts of a tooth
3.1.5 Present observations about teeth creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
3.2.1 Identify examples of foods in each food class
TB pp. 37-39 · AB pp. 22-25 · TB pp. 40-41 · AB pp. 26

1. Annotate the tooth outline with one observed change and explain how brushing helps clean that area.
2. Sort the cards and write another example beside every heading assigned.
Tooth model, washable food-residue marks, demonstration brush and tooth outlines.; Familiar food picture cards, food-class headings and example slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Return the annotated tooth outline and ask which surface was cleaned.
Point to the observed change before the individual explanation.
Practice and assessment
Check for a labelled part, a before-and-after observation and a care action linked to that part.
Annotate the tooth outline with one observed change and explain how brushing helps clean that area.
Closure
Ask pupils to name one routine they can explain to someone else.
Give a care action and link it to the tooth or gum area shown.
Set induction
Show pictures of rice and fish and ask how they could be placed into different food classes.
Name a likely class for each card.
Main activity
Model sorting single foods by the food class shown in the textbook. Give each group a small selection and the available class headings.
Sort each card under a heading and propose one further example for each assigned class.
Practice and assessment
Allocate two or three class headings per pupil, then check correct placement and one new example for each.
Sort the cards and write another example beside every heading assigned.
Closure
Ask for one way to justify a class choice when two foods look similar.
Name the food class and point to a named example that supports it.
references: TB pp. 37-39 · AB pp. 22-25 · TB pp. 40-41 · AB pp. 26

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain why food classes matter
details: 3.2.2 Draw conclusions about how each food class helps the body
1. Submit three class–role pairs and give a reason for one pair.
Food-class cards, function cards and short scenario slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Ask what food helps with when someone needs energy to move.
Propose a food class and give a reason.
Main activity
Model “class–role” with one example. Give groups short needs such as energy, growth or healthy digestion and cards to match.
Match food classes to their roles, then explain a match using one relevant body need.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to match three classes to three roles and justify one selection.
Submit three class–role pairs and give a reason for one pair.
Closure
Compare two distinct roles and ask for an example of each.
Name the classes and explain one difference in their roles.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Plan a balanced meal
details: 3.2.3 Use the food pyramid to explain examples of balanced meals
1. Draw or list a meal and explain why the selected components fit the food pyramid.
Food pyramid diagram, meal cards and plate templates.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a one-food meal picture and ask which parts of a balanced meal are missing.
Name one missing food group and propose a food example.
Main activity
Model using the food pyramid to check variety and relative proportions. Ask pairs to improve a simple meal while keeping it realistic.
Build a meal with cards, identify where each component fits in the pyramid and explain one revision.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil a blank plate. Check the proposed meal and its explanation against the pyramid.
Draw or list a meal and explain why the selected components fit the food pyramid.
Closure
Invite pupils to give one change that improves a sample meal.
Name the food added or adjusted and connect it to its place in the pyramid.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain an imbalanced diet
details:
3.2.4 Explain why an unbalanced diet can affect health
3.2.5 Present observations about food classes creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Annotate each menu with examples of food classes. Use the pyramid to compare the two menus over time.
Two illustrated menus, food pyramid and comparison slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two sample menus and ask which contains a wider variety of suitable foods.
Choose a menu and point to visible evidence.
Main activity
Guide groups to label the food classes represented in two menus. Model tying a repeated imbalance to one effect.
Annotate each menu with examples of food classes. Use the pyramid to compare the two menus over time.
Closure
Ask pupils to compare two menu cards against the food-class chart.
Identify one food class missing or underrepresented in one menu.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain an imbalanced diet / Describe digestion
details:
3.2.4 Explain why an unbalanced diet can affect health
3.2.5 Present observations about food classes creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
3.3.1 Describe how digestion breaks food down so the body can absorb nutrients

1. Label one food class in each menu. Explain one likely effect of the less balanced pattern and one change that addresses it.
2. Place cards in an evidence-based order and say how the body can make use of nutrients after breaking food down.
Two illustrated menus, food pyramid and comparison slips.; Food-piece illustrations, digestion sequence cards and a body diagram.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display the less balanced menu and its suggested change.
Name the food class addressed by that change.
Practice and assessment
Check a labelled food example, one possible effect of a repeated imbalance and a realistic change.
Label one food class in each menu. Explain one likely effect of the less balanced pattern and one change that addresses it.
Closure
Ask pupils why a single sample menu is different from a long-term diet.
Explain that repeated patterns affect the body over time.
Set induction
Ask whether the body can use a large piece of food in the same form it is swallowed.
Suggest what happens to food after chewing and swallowing.
Main activity
Use picture cards to model food breaking down into smaller components and show where digestion occurs. Build a simple class sequence without using real food.
Place cards in an evidence-based order and say how the body can make use of nutrients after breaking food down.
Closure
Show an intact food illustration beside its broken-down representation.
Describe one change caused by digestion.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Describe digestion
details: 3.3.1 Describe how digestion breaks food down so the body can absorb nutrients
1. Explain in simple terms what digestion changes and why that helps the body use nutrients.
Food-piece illustrations, digestion sequence cards and a body diagram.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a food particle diagram before and after breakdown.
Identify which representation shows smaller particles.
Practice and assessment
Invite each pupil to give a short oral or written explanation with both breakdown and purpose.
Explain in simple terms what digestion changes and why that helps the body use nutrients.
Closure
Ask a pupil to complete “Digestion breaks food down so …”.
Finish the sentence using a body-use or nutrients statement.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Trace the path of food
details: 3.3.2 Put the parts through which food passes during digestion in sequence
1. Order the five organs correctly and identify the anus as the exit for undigested waste.
Digestive-pathway diagram, movable organ labels and arrows.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show an outline of the human body and ask where food enters.
Point to the mouth and name a likely next place.
Main activity
Model following one continuous route using arrow cards. Give groups scrambled cards for the organs and the exit.
Arrange mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Add the exit and trace the full route.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil the unlabelled path and six movable labels, including the exit. Check order independently.
Order the five organs correctly and identify the anus as the exit for undigested waste.
Closure
Ask which organ follows the stomach along the route.
Point to and name the small intestine.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Trace the path of food
details: 3.3.2 Put the parts through which food passes during digestion in sequence
1. Arrange cards for mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and exit; explain the direction using arrows.
Digestive-pathway diagram, movable organ labels and arrows.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a mouth card and a stomach card from the digestive pathway.
Predict which is encountered first by food.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide an unlabelled digestive-system diagram and sequence cards.
Arrange cards for mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and exit; explain the direction using arrows.
Closure
Ask which organ follows the stomach in the labelled sequence.
Point to the small intestine and trace the direction of movement.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain what happens after digestion
details:
3.3.3 Draw a conclusion about what happens to food material the body does not need after digestion
3.3.4 Present observations about digestion creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Draw and label the two routes. Add a sentence about what happens to the material the body does not use.
Digestive diagram with coloured arrows, nutrient/waste cards and individual diagrams.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two arrows after the small intestine and ask what could travel by different routes.
Suggest what happens to useful nutrients and undigested material.
Main activity
Model two routes: nutrients through the wall of the small intestine into the blood, and remaining undigested food toward the exit.
Place nutrient and remaining-food cards on the two routes. Explain what each arrow carries.
Practice and assessment
Check arrows and a conclusion that the remaining undigested food goes through the large intestine and leaves as faeces.
Draw and label the two routes. Add a sentence about what happens to the material the body does not use.
Closure
Ask which arrow carries nutrients to the body.
Point to the route toward the blood and explain why the routes differ.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Humans
details:
3.1.1 Describe the different types of teeth and what each does
3.2.3 Use the food pyramid to explain examples of balanced meals
3.3.1 Describe how digestion breaks food down so the body can absorb nutrients
1. Make a map explaining how teeth start breaking food down, how a balanced meal supplies nutrients and how digestion lets the body use them.
Tooth images, meal cards, digestion route and concept-map sheet.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a tooth, a meal and a stomach picture. Ask for a connection between any two.
Explain one link using a fact from the unit.
Main activity
Model one connecting arrow with a verb. Ask pairs to place all three images and discuss how to connect them.
Sketch a concept map linking teeth, balanced food and digestion using words along the arrows.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil’s diagram has all three ideas and accurate labelled links.
Make a map explaining how teeth start breaking food down, how a balanced meal supplies nutrients and how digestion lets the body use them.
Closure
Ask which link explains why chewing helps.
Point to the relevant arrow and explain it in one sentence.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Group animals by what they eat
details:
4.1.1 Group animals by what they eat
4.1.2 Use examples to explain what herbivores, carnivores and omnivores eat
1. Classify the six animals as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores using the diet records.
Six animal pictures with diet records, group labels and classification grids.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a rabbit food card and a tiger food card and compare what the two animals eat.
Describe the food evidence for each card.
Main activity
Model how plant, animal or both kinds of food support the three diet groups. Give groups six illustrated cases with diet evidence.
Sort each case using the diet shown and record at least one piece of evidence for the classification.
Practice and assessment
Give an independent grid. Check six classifications and the evidence used instead of the animal’s appearance.
Classify the six animals as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores using the diet records.
Closure
Ask how the evidence changes when a card lists plants and animals.
Name omnivore and cite both types of food.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Infer the group from an animal's diet
details: 4.1.3 Infer an animal's group from evidence about its diet
1. Highlight plant and animal foods and infer the likely group from the full log.
Four-day feeding log cards, diet group chart and evidence slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a single feeding observation and ask what additional detail might help identify a diet group.
Say what food is recorded and propose what else to observe.
Main activity
Model reading a record across several days rather than relying on the animal’s shape. Give pairs an unfamiliar animal’s food log.
Highlight plant and animal foods and infer the likely group from the full log.
Closure
Show one animal's food log containing plant and animal foods.
Name the evidence needed before assigning a diet group.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Infer the group from an animal's diet / Compare animal teeth
details:
4.1.3 Infer an animal's group from evidence about its diet
4.1.4 Describe similarities and differences in the teeth of herbivores, carnivores and omnivores

1. State the likely group and quote or paraphrase one or two food observations that justify it.
2. Compare two features for each pictured group and connect one observed feature to the type of food eaten.
Four-day feeding log cards, diet group chart and evidence slips.; Clear tooth photos or diagrams of three animals, comparison grids and pencils.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Return an animal diet log with two highlighted foods.
Identify whether each food is plant or animal material.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil a second short record. Check that the conclusion names the correct group and cites recorded foods.
State the likely group and quote or paraphrase one or two food observations that justify it.
Closure
Ask whether a record of one meal is always enough to classify a diet.
Explain why more observations may change the inference.
Set induction
Compare two close-up tooth images and ask what looks alike or different.
Name a visible tooth feature without naming the diet yet.
Main activity
Set out herbivore, carnivore and omnivore diagrams with diet labels. Model comparing a broad grinding surface and a pointed tearing surface.
Compare two features for each pictured group and connect one observed feature to the type of food eaten.
Closure
Show a broad grinding tooth and a pointed tearing tooth.
Match one visible shape to a feeding function.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Compare animal teeth
details: 4.1.4 Describe similarities and differences in the teeth of herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
1. Complete the grid and relate one specific tooth feature to the animal’s diet.
Clear tooth photos or diagrams of three animals, comparison grids and pencils.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display a tooth comparison grid with one cell missing.
Choose a visible tooth feature to complete it.
Practice and assessment
Ask for an individual entry showing two comparisons across all three groups and one evidence-based link.
Complete the grid and relate one specific tooth feature to the animal’s diet.
Closure
Ask what information would confirm a prediction about diet made from teeth alone.
Propose checking what the animal is observed eating.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain evidence about animal diets
details: 4.1.5 Present observations about animals' diets creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Present a diet classification, name one supporting food observation and explain the behaviour change in the case.
Food record cards, a teacher-made before–after feeding scenario and presentation sheets.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show an animal feeding record with one change between two days.
Describe what changed in the record before suggesting why.
Main activity
Guide groups to separate the usual diet classification from a reported behaviour change. Model how to cite a recorded food item.
Prepare a brief report naming the group, a supporting observation and one possible reason for the observed change.

Identify Solar System members
details: 9.1.1 Use different media to identify the objects that make up the Solar System
1. Label a sequence from the Sun outwards and add asteroids and comets to the list of other objects.
Sun and planet cards, orbit strip and object cards for asteroids and comets.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the Sun and Earth cards and ask where the Sun belongs in the model.
Place the Sun centrally and identify Earth as a planet.
Main activity
Use the textbook sequence to check the eight planet cards. Demonstrate adding two other objects to an illustrated Solar System without treating them as planets.
Build the Sun and planet sequence, then sort asteroid and comet cards as separate object types.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil labels the Sun and eight planets in order and names two other object types.
Label a sequence from the Sun outwards and add asteroids and comets to the list of other objects.
Closure
Ask pupils to name Earth’s neighbouring planets in the order from the Sun.
Identify Venus and Mars from the completed order.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Compare planet temperatures
details: 9.1.2 Use the order of the planets to describe the general pattern in their temperatures
1. Submit a trend statement and one evidence-backed explanation of Venus as an exception.
Teacher-supplied chart of relative distances and representative temperatures, axes and comparison slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Ask which of Mercury and Venus is closer to the Sun before revealing the data.
Identify Mercury from the planet sequence and predict which might be hotter.
Main activity
Read both columns of the chart. Guide groups to describe the broad trend and compare Mercury and Venus using the chart and the textbook explanation of Venus’s atmosphere.
Order examples by distance, compare their temperatures and mark Venus as an exception to the simple distance prediction.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil states the general trend, cites Mercury/Venus evidence and links Venus’s high temperature to heat trapped by its atmosphere.
Submit a trend statement and one evidence-backed explanation of Venus as an exception.
Closure
Ask why distance is useful but insufficient in this example.
Explain that atmosphere can affect a planet’s temperature.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Compare planet temperatures
details: 9.1.2 Use the order of the planets to describe the general pattern in their temperatures
1. Arrange the planets in order from the Sun using a supplied chart, describe the general temperature pattern and identify Venus as an exception.
Teacher-supplied chart of relative distances and representative temperatures, axes and comparison slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show Venus and Earth on a planet chart.
Identify which planet is closer to the Sun before comparing temperatures.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide a checked planet-order and mean-temperature chart; guide comparison of the overall pattern, without requiring a detailed explanation of atmospheric physics.
Arrange the planets in order from the Sun using a supplied chart, describe the general temperature pattern and identify Venus as an exception.
Closure
Ask why temperature is not determined by distance alone.
Mention Venus's thick atmosphere and its heat-trapping effect.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Model orbits around the Sun
details: 9.1.3 Describe how planets move around the Sun along their orbits
1. Demonstrate the orbit and distinguish revolution from rotation in an explanation.
Tabletop Sun and planet models, a marked side of the planet ball and orbit arrows.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Spin the ball in place and ask whether it has travelled round the Sun.
Identify a spin without an orbit.
Main activity
Show rotation about the model’s axis and revolution around the Sun separately, then together. Set out an arrow track for partners to use.
Take turns modelling one complete orbit and one spin. Use the marked side to show the difference.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to identify and demonstrate both motions. Check the model travels around the Sun for revolution.
Demonstrate the orbit and distinguish revolution from rotation in an explanation.
Closure
Ask which motion determines a planet’s year in the model.
Point to the orbit and name revolution.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Model orbits around the Sun
details: 9.1.3 Describe how planets move around the Sun along their orbits
1. Move planet markers along their separate paths around a central Sun marker; draw and label the paths and describe the movement of planets around the Sun.
Tabletop Sun and planet models, a marked side of the planet ball and orbit arrows.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a ball turning in place and then moving around a marker.
Name the two different movements.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide a simple orbit diagram and model; distinguish the paths without requiring rotation as a separate assessed concept.
Move planet markers along their separate paths around a central Sun marker; draw and label the paths and describe the movement of planets around the Sun.
Closure
Ask pupils to draw an arrow for one orbit and one spin.
Label revolution and rotation correctly.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Compare revolution times
details: 9.1.4 Explain how distance from the Sun relates to the time a planet takes to complete an orbit
1. Produce the ordered list and state how the period generally changes with distance from the Sun.
Four printed planet data cards, number strip and distance labels.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two cards with different revolution periods and ask how they can be compared.
Identify the relevant values and check their units.
Main activity
Give four planets with periods in consistent units from a checked teaching chart. Model ordering one pair by period, then comparing distances.
Arrange planets from the shortest to longest period and use a separate distance row to look for a pattern.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil orders all four and gives a distance–period relationship supported by the cards.
Produce the ordered list and state how the period generally changes with distance from the Sun.
Closure
Ask what one revolution period measures.
Explain it is the time for one trip around the Sun.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Compare revolution times
details: 9.1.4 Explain how distance from the Sun relates to the time a planet takes to complete an orbit
1. Order four planets using a supplied orbital-period table and relate longer periods to greater distance from the Sun.
Four printed planet data cards, number strip and distance labels.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two orbital-period values from the table.
Identify which planet takes longer to complete an orbit.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide verified simplified orbital data and ask pupils to cite two entries.
Order four planets using a supplied orbital-period table and relate longer periods to greater distance from the Sun.
Closure
Ask for one pair of planets that supports the distance-period relationship.
Cite the two table entries and describe the pattern.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Communicate Solar System findings
details: 9.1.5 Present observations about the Solar System creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Explain the relationship in one minute or on a written card using both the diagram and the data point.
Planet diagrams, checked temperature or period chart, blank poster sheets and evidence prompts.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a planet claim without supporting evidence and ask what could strengthen it.
Suggest one matching data point or a labelled part of a model.
Main activity
Model combining a diagram with a number or recorded comparison. Invite pairs to present one relationship about planet temperature, distance or revolution.
Prepare a labelled diagram and select a data point that directly supports the explanation.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil names the relationship, labels the diagram accurately and points to a matching data point.
Explain the relationship in one minute or on a written card using both the diagram and the data point.
Closure
Ask the class to identify the evidence in one presentation.
Name the relevant label or data point and say how it supports the idea.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Identify a pulley and its purpose
details: 10.1.1 Describe what a pulley is and what it is used for
1. Label the wheel and rope and explain one way the pulley helps move a load.
Fixed pulley demonstration, light attached load and outline cards.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a photo of a flag raising system and ask what guides the line.
Identify the wheel or rope in the picture.
Main activity
Point out the wheel and rope on a secure tabletop demonstration. Slowly raise the light load and trace the moving line.
Observe the demonstration, trace the rope over the wheel and tell a partner what the pulley helps people move.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil an outline to label. Check wheel, rope and a correct purpose statement.
Label the wheel and rope and explain one way the pulley helps move a load.
Closure
Ask how the line moves when the load goes up.
Use the demonstration to describe one direction of motion.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain a fixed pulley
details: 10.1.2 Use a model to explain how a fixed pulley works
1. Draw a downward pull arrow and an upward load arrow. Explain that the pulley changes the direction of the pull.
Secure fixed pulley stands, soft cords, very light test loads and arrow cards.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Hold a pulley diagram and ask which way to pull to make the load rise.
Predict the pull and movement directions with two arrows.
Main activity
Demonstrate changing the direction of pull using a secure model. Give pairs a checked station with a light test load.
Pull the line down under supervision, observe the load rise and mark arrows on the model drawing.
Practice and assessment
Check the pull and load arrows on a new sketch. Ask what the single fixed pulley changes in this demonstration.
Draw a downward pull arrow and an upward load arrow. Explain that the pulley changes the direction of the pull.
Closure
Ask what the direction arrows can show about this model.
State the two directions indicated by the labelled arrows.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Explain a fixed pulley
details: 10.1.2 Use a model to explain how a fixed pulley works
1. On a fixed-pulley model, draw arrows for pulling down and the load moving up; explain the change in direction.
Secure fixed pulley stands, soft cords, very light test loads and arrow cards.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a flagpole rope passing over a fixed pulley.
Predict the flag's movement if the free end is pulled downward.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Use a safe light load on a securely fixed model, or use a diagram.
On a fixed-pulley model, draw arrows for pulling down and the load moving up; explain the change in direction.
Closure
Ask pupils to point to the direction of effort and load movement.
Draw arrows showing opposite directions in the fixed pulley.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Find pulley applications
details: 10.1.3 Give everyday examples of how people use pulleys
1. List three applications and connect a named benefit to the task the pulley helps perform.
Photos of flagpoles, blinds, wells and other checked examples, scenario cards and labels.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a flagpole rope and ask how it differs from lifting the flag directly by hand.
Name one practical benefit of the pulley position.
Main activity
Ask groups to identify the wheel, rope and load in illustrated uses. Provide picture options with and without pulleys to compare.
Find how the parts work in each use and record a practical benefit in one case.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil identifies three genuine applications and explains a benefit in one context.
List three applications and connect a named benefit to the task the pulley helps perform.
Closure
Ask for evidence that one chosen example really uses a pulley.
Point to the wheel and rope arrangement in its image.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Find pulley applications
details: 10.1.3 Give everyday examples of how people use pulleys
1. Match flagpole, well and construction-hoist pictures to pulley use; explain one benefit in the selected example.
Photos of flagpoles, blinds, wells and other checked examples, scenario cards and labels.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a well bucket and a flagpole with pulley pictures.
Identify the shared simple machine.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide three contextual diagrams and ask pupils to justify the match.
Match flagpole, well and construction-hoist pictures to pulley use; explain one benefit in the selected example.
Closure
Ask which pulley application would help raise a flag.
Choose the flagpole and explain the change in direction of pull.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Build and explain a pulley model
details:
10.1.4 Build a working pulley model
10.1.5 Present observations about pulleys creatively through writing, speech, drawings or digital tools
1. Show the load rise in the test. Draw the wheel, rope and load with arrows for pull and load motion.
Teacher-checked pulley kits, soft cords, clamps, arrow cards and very light test loads.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a secure model and ask what would stop the load from rising smoothly.
Name one possible threading or alignment problem.
Main activity
Check support and rope placement before testing. Assign a builder and an observer, then switch roles for a second test.
Assemble and test the model with a light load. Record the observed motion, then swap roles and check the rope path.
Practice and assessment
Observe the pair lift the load. Ask each pupil for an individual sketch with a supported explanation.
Show the load rise in the test. Draw the wheel, rope and load with arrows for pull and load motion.
Closure
Ask which change had a visible effect on the model’s performance.
Describe an adjustment and the observed result.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 3 SK
Solar System and Machine
details:
9.1.3 Describe how planets move around the Sun along their orbits
10.1.2 Use a model to explain how a fixed pulley works
1. Explain the orbit and add pull and load arrows with an explanation of how the fixed pulley changes direction.
Orbit diagram, small fixed-pulley model or diagram, arrow cards and two-question review sheet.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display an orbit drawing and a pulley drawing. Ask what travels in each.
Identify the planet and the pulley load in their different models.
Main activity
Review the centre and motion of an orbit and demonstrate the direction of pull and load movement. Give a new diagram for each topic.
Read the orbit diagram and place arrows for the demonstrated fixed pulley in pairs.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil interprets one orbit representation and correctly explains the relation of pull to load movement.
Explain the orbit and add pull and load arrows with an explanation of how the fixed pulley changes direction.
Closure
Ask pupils to name one useful label in each model.
Name the Sun and the load or pull direction and explain what each label shows.
